opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful, but I wouldn't say it's the most important thing. In a young field, people naturally use the same term to mean slightly different things, and that's okay. Some people think of a world model as something that predicts the next frame of video. Others think of it as an internal representation an agent uses to plan. Others think of it as a simulator you can use to train robots or autonomous vehicles. These views overlap a lot, and the boundaries are still moving.

What matters more to me is whether we agree on what problem we're trying to solve. For me, a world model is a model that, given the current state of the world and some action, can predict how the world will evolve. If you have that, you can use it to imagine, to plan, and to generate training data for physical AI. That's the capability we care about, whatever we call it.

A shared definition becomes more important when you want to measure progress. If everyone defines it differently, it's hard to build benchmarks, compare results, or tell whether the field is moving forward or just renaming things. So over time I think the community will converge, the way it did with terms like "foundation model." But I'd rather people spend their energy building systems that actually work in the physical world, and let the definition sharpen as we learn what works. Often the definition comes after the breakthroughs, not before.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts the community will converge on a shared definition over time; it does not say agreement will remain elusive as with AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think it's that important, honestly. In the research community right now, "world model" means slightly different things to different people, and I'm fine with that. For some, a world model is a video generation model that predicts the next frames. For others, it's a latent model that only predicts the abstract state and never renders pixels. For a roboticist, it might be the thing that lets a policy imagine the consequences of an action before taking it. These are different objects, but they're all pointing at the same underlying idea: a model that has learned how the world evolves, and that you can query to simulate what happens next.

I actually think a strict shared definition at this stage would slow us down. When a field is young, the definitions should follow the results, not the other way around. If we had sat down in 2017 and tried to agree on what a "language model" was supposed to be before building them, we would have argued about whether it needed grounding, whether it needed a knowledge base, whether next-token prediction counted as understanding. Instead people just built them and scaled them, and the definition sorted itself out through what turned out to be useful.

What I do think matters is being precise about what your particular model does and how you measure it. If you say you've built a world model, tell me what it takes as input, what it predicts, over what horizon, and whether it respects physics. Those are the things that let two groups compare work. So my view is: less energy on the shared word, more energy on shared benchmarks and shared evaluation. The word "world model" is really a direction, a bet that simulating the world is the path to physical AI, the same way simulating text was the path to language AI. We can all agree on the direction even while we disagree on the details.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people currently use “world model” differently and argues against forcing a shared definition, but it does not predict that agreement will remain elusive or compare this to defining AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to be clear about what we mean, but I don’t think everyone needs to agree on one definition before we can make progress. People use “world model” to describe different things. Are we talking about a model that generates plausible videos, or a model that predicts how an environment changes when an agent takes an action? Those are related, but they imply different capabilities and different ways to evaluate success.

So, for me, the useful part of a shared definition is making those assumptions explicit. What does the model observe? What can it predict? And can those predictions help us make better decisions? If we agree on those questions, we can have a productive conversation even if our definitions are a little different.

r001.rationale: The response says people use different definitions and that agreement on one definition is not necessary, but it does not predict that agreement will remain elusive or compare the issue to defining AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important, but I don’t think we need everyone to agree on one definition before we can make progress. People use “world model” to mean different things. Some mean a model that predicts future observations; others mean a model that lets an agent understand how its actions will affect the environment.

For me, the useful common ground is prediction: given what we’ve observed, and perhaps an action we might take, can the model predict what happens next? Then we can be more specific about the capabilities we need. Does it capture physical interactions? Can it maintain a consistent world over time? Can you use it for planning?

So a shared definition helps us communicate and compare results. But I’d put more emphasis on agreeing on the problems and how we measure progress than on finding a definition that covers everything.

r001.rationale: The response notes that people use different definitions and says a universal definition is not necessary for progress, but it does not predict that agreement will remain elusive or compare this to defining AGI.
